question: Does a stop expressed in the instrument's own volatility behave better than a fixed fraction?

design.statement: A volatility-scaled stop should make the first-bar exit rate consistent across instruments; a fixed fraction should not.

interpretation: The structural prediction held and the return improvement did not. Scaling the stop to trailing volatility cut the spread of first-bar exit rates across instruments from 0.182 to 0.041, so the stop does come to mean the same thing everywhere. But the multiple that led the development window, 1.5x, returned +0.449% there at t = 2.18 and -0.678% on the holdout at t = -2.94, a complete reversal. Choosing a multiple from history is the same noise as choosing a geometry from history, which this work has now reproduced four times. One result replicates in both windows: a tight stop at 0.5x sigma loses -0.300% and -0.243% at t = -4.96 and -3.13. The shipped 2% stop sits in that regime, closing 73% of episodes in their first bar.
limitations: Four multiples were tested; the best on development is expected to flatter itself.
Episode counts differ between arms because a wider stop changes which signals resolve, so arms are not paired.
Trailing sigma over twenty bars is one estimator among many and was not varied.
